questions.stem: Kemar Reid must present a proposal to his hotel's management team. What should he decide first?
options: Which slide template and colours look most modern
How many slides he can fit in
Which jokes to open with
What he wants the audience to know, feel or do

questions.stem: Which question is most useful when analysing the audience for a presentation?
options: What colour are the walls of the room painted?
What do they know, and what do they need?
How many slides did the last speaker use with them?
Which font and colours do I personally like best?

questions.stem: Ms Campbell will present the results of a new service first to the board and then to frontline staff. How should the two versions differ?
options: Board: cost and risk; staff: what changes in daily work
Both versions should be exactly the same, word for word
The staff version should use many more technical terms

questions.stem: Which structure suits most business presentations?
options: Start with the details, then give the main point at the very end
Present the slides in any order and let the audience sort them
Opening, key points with evidence, then a clear close
Read the full report aloud from the first page to the last

questions.stem: Which opening is most likely to get a busy audience's attention?
options: An apology for being nervous and not well prepared
A relevant fact or question tied to their concerns
A long list of the speaker's qualifications and past jobs
Reading out the agenda slide word for word, slowly

questions.stem: Why do experienced presenters often limit a talk to about three key messages?
options: Because the slide software allows only three sections
Because audiences do not like to hear more than three numbers
Because three points is a rule set by company law
Because people remember a few points better

questions.stem: What is the main benefit of storyboarding a presentation on paper before building the slides?
options: It fixes the flow before time goes into design
It means the presenter will not need to rehearse later
It lets the presenter skip the research on the topic
It makes sure the slides will print well in colour

questions.stem: Which slide works best for a projected presentation to 40 people?
options: A full paragraph of 120 words in small print
Ten bullet points, each a long sentence
One heading, a few key words and a clear image
Four charts and a table squeezed onto one slide

questions.stem: For body text on slides projected in a training room, which font size is generally recommended?
options: 10 to 12 point
About 24 point or larger
Any size, as long as it fits
8 point, to fit more information

questions.stem: Which colour choice makes slide text easiest to read for everyone, including people with colour-vision differences?

Yellow text on a white background

A pie chart

A single photograph

It makes the chart too easy for the audience to read

questions.stem: Andre wants to use a photo he found online in a presentation to clients. What should he do?
options: Use it, because anything online is free to use
Use it, as long as he crops out the watermark

Round it up to make it more impressive

questions.stem: A presentation will be shared online afterwards. Which step makes it more accessible to people with visual impairments?

Making the text fly in with lots of animation
Adding alternative text to every image
Using small, light grey text to keep the slides tidy

questions.stem: When is it usually best to give out a detailed handout at a business presentation?
options: Before the start, so people read it while you speak
At the end, unless they need it to follow the figures

Halfway through, to wake the audience up

questions.stem: Simone has a 20-minute slot, including 5 minutes for questions. She plans 10 content slides. How long, on average, can she spend on each slide?
options: 2 minutes
1 minute
2.5 minutes

questions.stem: A speaker talks at about 125 words a minute and has 12 minutes for the talk. About how many words should her notes cover at most?

options: Read through the slides silently once, the night before
Learn the script word for word so you never look up
Practise aloud with the slides and a timer, before a colleague
Skip practice entirely so the talk sounds more natural

Bringing a second presenter who can talk without slides
Asking the audience to come back on another day instead
Relying on the venue's computer to have the file

questions.stem: Which is the best way to manage nerves before presenting?
options: Drink several cups of strong coffee just before for energy
Avoid looking at the audience at all

questions.stem: Which use of voice helps an audience follow the key points?
options: Speaking in the same tone throughout
Speaking very quickly to show how confident you are
Speaking quietly so people lean in
Varying pace and pausing after key points

questions.stem: Which body language best supports a confident presentation?
options: Standing behind the screen with arms folded
Open posture, steady eye contact and natural gestures
Facing the screen and reading the slides aloud to the room
Pacing quickly up and down the room

questions.stem: What is the best way to use notes during a presentation?

Read a full typed script word for word from start to end
Read each slide aloud exactly

questions.stem: An audience member asks a question the presenter cannot answer. What should she do?
options: Make up an answer that sounds right and move on quickly
Ignore the question and move on
Say she will find out and reply by a set time

options: Argue back firmly until the resident accepts the fee

Pretend not to hear the comment and carry on talking

So she has time to think of a reason not to answer it

So the session runs on longer than the time allowed

options: Keep the camera off the whole time to save data

So questions are gathered without distracting her

questions.stem: A group of four will present a joint proposal. What makes the handovers between speakers smooth?
options: Each person designs slides in their own style
Each speaker repeats all the previous speaker's points in full
Speakers decide on the day who goes next

questions.stem: Which order suits a persuasive presentation asking a board to fund a new project?
options: Problem, solution, benefits and costs, then the ask
Benefits only, leaving the costs for another meeting
A history of the company, then thanks to the board

questions.stem: Which supporting evidence is most persuasive to a finance committee?
options: The presenter's strong personal feeling that it will work
A single story about one very happy customer last year
Costed figures from a reliable source
Several slides of attractive photos of the new product

questions.stem: How should animations and slide transitions be used in a business presentation?
options: On every bullet point, with a sound effect for each
Sparingly, only where they help explain a point
Never, under any circumstances
Randomly, to keep the audience guessing

questions.stem: How can a presenter best judge whether the presentation met its objective?
options: Count how many slides were shown in the time
Ask a friend afterwards if she looked good on stage
Time how long the applause went on at the end
Compare outcome and feedback with the objective

questions.stem: Twenty attendees scored a presentation out of 5. The scores add up to 84. What is the average score?
Of 45 people who completed a feedback form, 36 rated the presentation "clear" or "very clear". What percentage is that?

options: Keep them in, since the partners like to see detail
Remove them and share only approved data
Leave them in, but make the figures blurred and small

questions.stem: Which practice makes a presentation more inclusive for a mixed audience?
options: Using in-jokes that only some staff understand
Using slang and abbreviations without explaining them
Speaking only to the most senior people in the room
Plain language, explained terms and a variety of examples

questions.stem: What is the best way to close a presentation to a sales team?
options: Sum up the key points and state the action needed
Say "That's all, folks" and switch off the projector at once
Introduce a new topic not covered earlier

questions.stem: Why should a presenter use one template or slide master for the whole deck?
options: So that every slide can have a different font and colour
So the slides can be printed faster
So headings, colours and fonts stay consistent
So the file can never be edited

questions.stem: A slide must show a 12-row table of budget figures. What is the best approach?
options: Show the whole table in tiny print and read every number
Highlight the key figures; put the table in a handout
Leave the figures out of the presentation altogether

questions.stem: At rehearsal, a 15-minute talk runs to 22 minutes. What should the presenter do?
options: Speak faster on the day
Drop the questions session
Keep it and hope the chair allows extra time
Cut or shorten the least important content

questions.stem: What is the best reason for a presenter to arrive early at the venue?
options: To test equipment and greet people as they come
To take the best seat in the room before others arrive
To change the agenda without telling the organiser
To start making the slides for the presentation

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

essays.stem: You have been asked to give a 20-minute presentation to the board of a Kingston manufacturing firm, recommending a move to solar power. Describe how you would plan the presentation, from setting the objective to the final structure.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start with a clear objective: by the end, the board will approve a feasibility study and a budget for solar panels on the main factory. Next I would analyse the audience. Board members care about cost, risk, payback and reputation, and some may doubt the technology, so I would find out their concerns from the company secretary. I would then research reliable evidence: our electricity bills for two years, quotes from two installers, the expected savings and maintenance costs, and examples from similar firms. From this I would choose three key messages: the current cost of power, the savings and payback, and how risks such as hurricanes would be managed. I would storyboard the talk on paper: an opening with one striking figure, such as last year's power bill; a section for each key message with a chart; a summary; and the decision I need. I would plan 15 minutes for the talk and 5 for questions, prepare a one-page handout of the figures, and rehearse with a timer before a colleague.
markingPoints: Sets a clear, measurable objective
Analyses the board's interests and concerns
Gathers reliable evidence and selects a few key messages
Builds a logical structure with an opening, evidence and a clear request
Plans timing, handout and rehearsal

essays.stem: Explain how you would analyse the audience and adapt the same content on a new staff leave system for (a) senior managers and (b) frontline staff.
essays.modelAnswer: I would ask the same questions about each audience: what they already know, what they care about, what they must do after the talk, and what worries them. Senior managers will want to know why the system was chosen, what it costs, how it reduces errors and absence, what risks there are and what decisions they must make, such as approving the start date. For them I would keep the talk short, lead with the business case and figures, use a few clear charts and leave time for questions on cost and risk. Frontline staff will want to know how to apply for leave, what changes for them, when it starts and where to get help. They may worry that the system is harder to use or that their leave balance will change. For them I would use plain words, a step-by-step demonstration on screen, screenshots in a handout and examples from their own work, and I would answer concerns openly. The facts stay the same, but the emphasis, detail, language and examples change for each group.
markingPoints: Uses clear audience analysis questions
Identifies senior managers' needs: business case, cost, risk, decisions
Identifies frontline staff's needs: how to use it, what changes, concerns
Adapts structure, language, visuals and examples for each
Keeps the facts consistent across both versions

essays.stem: Describe the principles of good slide design for a business presentation and explain why each helps the audience.
essays.modelAnswer: First, each slide should carry one main idea with a clear heading that states the point, because the audience can then follow the argument at a glance. Second, text should be short: key words rather than full sentences, perhaps following the six-by-six rule, so that people listen to the speaker instead of reading. Third, text must be large enough to read from the back, about 24 point or more for body text, with strong contrast such as dark text on a light background; this also helps people with poor sight or colour-vision differences. Fourth, the deck should use one template, with the same fonts, colours and layout, so that it looks professional and nothing distracts. Fifth, visuals should explain rather than decorate: a well-labelled chart, a diagram or a relevant photo that the presenter has the right to use. Sixth, animation should be used sparingly, only to build up a point step by step. Finally, detailed tables belong in a handout, with only the key figures on the slide.
markingPoints: One idea per slide with a clear heading
Short text so the audience listens to the speaker
Readable size and strong contrast, including for visual differences
Consistent template and purposeful visuals with permission to use
Sparing animation and detail moved to handouts

essays.stem: A tourism officer must present three years of visitor numbers, spending per visitor and complaint rates to a parish committee. Explain how she should choose and design the charts so that the data is clear and honest.
essays.modelAnswer: She should first decide the message for each set of figures, because the chart must show that message. Visitor numbers over three years show a trend, so a line chart or a simple column chart by year works best. Spending per visitor could be shown as columns by year, perhaps with the figure in J$ printed on each bar so no one has to guess. Complaint rates should be shown as a rate, for example complaints per 1,000 visitors, so that a rise in visitors does not make complaints seem worse than they are. Each chart should have a heading that states the finding, labelled axes with units, a source and date, and no more colours than needed. To stay honest, the vertical axis should normally start at zero, the scales should be the same when charts are compared, and no year should be left out to hide a poor result. Three-dimensional effects should be avoided because they distort size. She should put the full table in a handout and practise explaining each chart in one or two sentences.
markingPoints: Chooses chart types to match the message (trend, comparison)
Uses rates rather than raw counts where fair
Adds clear headings, labelled axes, units and sources
Keeps charts honest: zero baseline, consistent scales, no omitted data or 3D effects
Supports the charts with a handout and a short explanation

essays.stem: Explain how voice, body language and the use of notes affect a presentation's success, and describe how a presenter can improve each.
essays.modelAnswer: Voice carries the message and the speaker's confidence. A flat, fast or quiet voice loses the audience, while varied pace and tone and a pause after each key point help people follow and remember. A presenter can improve by recording a rehearsal, listening back, marking pauses in the notes and practising slowing down at the start, when nerves make people rush. Body language affects whether the audience trusts the speaker. An open posture, steady eye contact around the room and natural gestures show confidence; folded arms, reading from the screen or pacing distract and suggest nerves. A presenter can improve by rehearsing in front of a colleague or on video, standing where the audience can see both her and the screen, and choosing a few people in different parts of the room to look at. Notes keep the talk on track, but reading a script word for word breaks contact with the audience. Brief cue cards or presenter notes with key words and figures are better, and good rehearsal means only a glance is needed.
markingPoints: Explains the effect of voice and how to improve it
Explains the effect of body language and eye contact
Gives practical ways to improve body language
Explains how notes help or hinder, favouring brief cues
Links improvement to rehearsal and feedback

essays.stem: Explain how a presenter should prepare for and handle questions from the audience, including difficult or hostile questions.
essays.modelAnswer: Preparation starts with the audience analysis: the presenter should list the questions they are likely to ask, especially awkward ones on cost, risk or fairness, and prepare short answers and any back-up slides or figures. She should tell the audience at the start when questions will be taken. When a question comes, she should listen fully, then repeat or rephrase it so everyone hears it and she can check she has understood. Answers should be brief, honest and linked back to the key messages. If she does not know the answer, she should say so and promise to reply by a set time, then do it. For a hostile question, she should stay calm, avoid arguing, acknowledge the person's concern, and answer the issue rather than the tone, with facts. If someone keeps interrupting, she can offer to meet them afterwards so others have a turn. Confidential matters should not be discussed in public. Finally, she should watch the time and close the session with a short summary of the main point.
markingPoints: Prepares likely questions, answers and back-up material
Listens, then repeats or rephrases the question
Gives brief, honest answers and follows up on unknowns
Handles hostile questions calmly, acknowledging concerns
Manages time and closes with a summary, protecting confidential matters

essays.stem: Compare delivering a presentation in person and on a video call, and describe how a presenter should prepare for each.
essays.modelAnswer: In person, the presenter can read the room, use the whole body, move closer to the audience and react at once to puzzled faces. The risks are the venue: equipment, lighting, sound and seating. On a video call, the audience may be spread across the island, which saves travel and time, but attention is harder to keep, body language is limited to the face and voice, and technical problems such as poor internet or sound can stop the talk. For an in-person talk, the presenter should visit or call the venue, test the projector and sound with her own laptop, arrive early, bring a back-up copy and printed notes, and plan where to stand. For a video call, she should test the platform, camera, microphone and screen sharing in advance; use a quiet, well-lit space; close other programs and notifications; look at the camera when speaking; make slides simpler with larger text; build in questions or polls every few minutes; and ask a colleague to manage the chat and the technology. In both cases, rehearsal in the same setting is essential.
markingPoints: Identifies advantages and limits of in-person delivery
Identifies advantages and limits of video calls
Describes preparation for the venue and equipment in person
Describes preparation for a video call (testing, setting, interaction, support)
Notes rehearsal in the real setting for both

essays.stem: A presenter has a 45-minute slot, which must include a 5-minute introduction by the chair and 10 minutes for questions. Her draft has 24 content slides, and in rehearsal she takes about 2 minutes per slide. Work out whether the talk fits, and recommend what she should change.
essays.modelAnswer: Time available for her talk is 45 − 5 − 10 = 30 minutes. Her draft needs 24 × 2 = 48 minutes, so it is 18 minutes too long. Checking: 48 − 30 = 18. At about 2 minutes per slide, 30 minutes allows about 15 content slides, so she must remove or combine about 9 slides. Speaking faster is not the answer, because it would make the talk harder to follow. She should go back to her objective and key messages and keep only the slides that support them. Detailed tables and background could go into a handout or back-up slides kept after the closing slide, to use only if a question needs them. Similar slides could be combined, for example three slides of monthly figures replaced by one chart. She could also shorten the opening. After the changes, she should rehearse again with a timer and aim to finish in about 28 minutes, leaving a small margin, because talks often run longer on the day. She should not cut the questions, since the board needs them to decide.
markingPoints: Calculates 30 minutes available and 48 minutes needed
Identifies the 18-minute overrun and about 15 slides to keep (cut about 9)
Rejects speaking faster and cuts by priority against key messages
Moves detail to a handout or back-up slides and combines slides
Re-rehearses with a margin and keeps the question time

essays.stem: After presenting a proposal to a hotel's management team, explain how you would evaluate the presentation and use the results to improve your next one.
essays.modelAnswer: I would begin with the objective I set: for example, the team was to approve a pilot of a new guest feedback app. The first test is the outcome: did they approve it, ask for changes or turn it down, and why? I would then gather feedback. I could give a short form asking how clear, convincing and well-timed the talk was, with a space for comments, and work out the average scores. I would also ask one or two trusted managers for honest views, and note the questions asked, because many questions on one point show it was not explained well. I would reflect on my own performance using my notes and, if it was recorded with permission, a video: did I keep to time, speak clearly, use the slides well and handle questions confidently? I would compare all this with the objective and list what worked and what to change, for example fewer slides on background and a clearer cost slide. Finally, I would make a short improvement plan with two or three actions and use it when preparing the next presentation.
markingPoints: Measures the outcome against the objective
Gathers audience feedback, including scores and comments
Uses the questions asked as evidence
Reflects on own delivery, with a recording only with permission
Writes an improvement plan with specific actions

essays.stem: Explain the legal and ethical points a presenter must consider when preparing a presentation for an outside audience, including images, data and confidential information. Refer to laws by their general purpose only.
essays.modelAnswer: Images, music, video and text belong to their creators. Intellectual property law, including copyright, protects them, so the presenter should use material she has created, material the organisation has licensed, or material whose licence allows such use, and credit the source where required. A logo or brand of another firm should not be used in a way that suggests a link that does not exist. Data must be accurate and honestly presented. Figures should come from reliable sources, be dated and credited, and charts must not exaggerate or hide results, because misleading an audience is unethical and could harm the organisation's reputation or lead to legal claims. Personal information about staff or customers is protected by the data protection law, so names, photos or details should not appear unless consent has been given or the information is made anonymous. Confidential business information, such as prices, salaries or plans, should be removed unless the organisation has approved its release. Finally, the presenter should avoid statements that could unfairly damage another person's or firm's reputation, and should treat all groups respectfully.
markingPoints: Respects intellectual property: licensed or own material, credited
Presents data accurately and honestly, with sources
Protects personal information in line with the data protection law's purpose
Removes confidential business information unless approved
Avoids damaging statements about others and shows respect

practical1.title: Design and deliver a persuasive presentation with slides
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a short brief from a made-up Jamaican organisation, for example: persuade a hotel's management to fund a staff wellness programme, persuade a parish committee to back a community market day, or persuade a company board to move to paperless invoicing. The brief names the audience and gives some facts and costs in J$. As a group, design and deliver a real 15-minute presentation with slides, followed by 5 minutes of questions from the assessor and other trainees, who act as the audience. First, write a one-page plan with the objective, an audience analysis and three key messages. Next, storyboard the talk on paper. Then build a deck of 8 to 12 slides on a computer, using one template, readable text, at least one chart made from the figures (checked twice) and only images you have the right to use. Rehearse once with a timer. Then deliver the presentation, with every member presenting one section and handing over smoothly, and answer the questions. Give each member a named role: lead presenter (writes the objective, opens and closes), audience analyst (writes the audience analysis and prepares likely questions), slide designer (builds the template and checks design rules), data officer (makes the chart and checks every figure), and timekeeper and rehearsal lead (runs the rehearsal and keeps time on the day). In a group of four, the lead presenter also keeps time. Photograph each stage.
materials: Presentation brief, audience and facts from the assessor
Computers with presentation software, a projector or large screen, and a clicker if available
Paper and markers for the storyboard; cue cards
photos: The one-page plan with objective, audience analysis and key messages
The finished slides on screen (one photo of the title slide and one of the chart)
Each member presenting their section (slides and speaker, or slides only if a member prefers no photo)
The question session and the list of questions the group prepared for
checklist: Took a named role and presented one section
Objective and key messages suit the audience named in the brief
Slides are clear: one idea each, readable text, consistent template, honest chart
Figures on the slides are correct and were checked twice
Spoke clearly, with eye contact and few glances at notes
Group kept within the 15 minutes for the talk
safety: Use only the made-up organisation and figures, and only images the group has the right to use
Tape down or route cables away from walkways and the presenting area
Ask permission before photographing anyone; photograph the slides if a member prefers no photo
Give and receive questions and feedback respectfully, and support members who are nervous

practical2.title: Deliver a data briefing presentation and evaluate it
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a data pack from a made-up organisation, such as a guest house's quarterly results, a ministry service centre's waiting times or a school's attendance figures, with a short request: brief the staff on what the figures show and what will change. As a group, prepare and deliver a real 10-minute briefing with slides to other trainees acting as staff, followed by 5 minutes of questions. Turn the key figures into two or three charts (each figure checked twice), build 6 to 10 slides, and prepare a one-page handout with the full table. Deliver the briefing, with every member presenting a part. Then give the audience a short feedback form with four questions scored 1 to 5. Work out the average score for each question (checked twice), and write a one-page evaluation comparing the result with your objective, with three improvements. Give each member a named role: briefing lead (sets the objective and opens and closes), data analyst (picks the key figures and makes the charts), slide and handout designer (builds the deck and handout), question lead (prepares for likely questions and chairs the question time), and evaluation officer (designs the feedback form, works the averages and drafts the evaluation with the group). In a group of four, the briefing lead also chairs the questions. Photograph each stage.
materials: Data pack and request from the assessor
Computers with presentation and spreadsheet software, a projector or large screen, and a printer
Paper feedback forms (or a simple online form) and pens
photos: The objective and the key figures chosen from the data pack
The charts on screen, with the second check of the figures marked
The handout and the slide deck
Each member presenting their part (slides and speaker, or slides only if a member prefers no photo)
The completed feedback forms and the calculation of averages
The one-page evaluation with three improvements
checklist: Took a named role and presented part of the briefing
Charts suit the data, are labelled and honest, and the figures are correct
Slides and handout are clear and consistent, with detail kept in the handout
Delivered their part clearly, at a steady pace, within the time
Handled at least one question well (listened, rephrased, answered or promised a reply)
Averages are correct and checked twice; evaluation compares results with the objective
safety: Treat the data pack as confidential and use only the made-up names and figures
Feedback forms are anonymous; do not record who gave which score
Keep cables taped down and the presenting area clear
Ask permission before photographing anyone, and give feedback on the work, not the person
